newsitem.title: USA: Ohio Gov. forms task force on school funding.
newsitem.headline: Ohio Gov. forms task force on school funding.

text.p: Ohio Gov. George Voinovich has created a task force to study the state school funding formula in the wake of last week's Ohio Supreme Court ruling that found the current system unconstitutional.

Voinovich, legislative leaders, the state superintendent of public instruction and the state budget director will serve on the task force, which will present its recommendations to the General Assembly, the governor said in a news release Friday.
"It is crucial that we move responsibly, but promptly, in order to give the legislature ample time to consider the input from the task force," Voinovich said.

Ohio Attorney General Betty Montgomery believes the supreme court decision could lead to "years" and possibly decades of litigation based on funding reforms in other states, spokesman Todd Boyer said Monday.

"Texas and New Jersey decisions handed down years and sometimes decades ago are still subject of litigation, which leads the attorney general to believe that scenario is realistic for Ohio," Boyer said.
While the Supreme Court specifically noted what the legislature should not do, it was "much less specific" on a proper funding approach, Boyer said.

The supreme court gave state officials one year to overhaul the funding system after finding that the current method violates the state constitution's requirement of a thorough and efficient system of common schools throughout the state.

The Ohio Coalition for Equity and Adequacy of School Funding, which represents school districts that brought the lawsuit, also plans to offer recommendations for overhauling the system on April 15, Executive Director William Phillis said Monday.
The ruling has resulted in "a lot of confusion," Phillis said, noting that he has been conducting a number of informational meetings around Ohio.
Voinovich said last week that the supreme court decision essentially called for a massive tax hike and added that it could erode "the long-standing tradition of local decision making."
Rating agency officials have said the ruling would not have any immediate affect on ratings for the state or school districts.
The supreme court made clear in its 4-3 ruling that it did not advocate taking money from more affluent districts to address the needs of poorer school districts.
